references.text: God repeats the promise to take Israel as His own possession at Mount Sinai, expanding it to call them a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.
The covenant formula 'I will be your God, and you shall be my people' is repeated as part of the blessings for obedience.
Moses reminds the people that the Lord brought them out of Egypt, the iron furnace, to make them His own possession.
Israel is confirmed as a holy people, chosen by the Lord to be His own possession above all peoples on earth.
The renewal of the covenant in Moab confirms that the Lord takes Israel as His people and will be their God, just as He promised the fathers.
Jeremiah prophesies about the new covenant where the Lord will again be their God and they shall be His people, with the law written in their hearts.
Ezekiel repeats the covenant formula in connection with the promise of spiritual renewal and cleansing of the people.
In the vision of the dry bones, God promises that He will dwell among them, be their God, and they shall be His people.
Hosea prophesies about restoration where God will say to 'Not my people': 'You are my people', and they shall answer: 'My God'.
Zechariah repeats the covenant formula in the context of Israel's future salvation and restoration.
Paul quotes the covenant formula and applies it to the church as God's temple, where God dwells among His people.
The Letter to the Hebrews quotes Jeremiah 31 and the new covenant promise that the Lord will be their God and they shall be His people.
Peter applies covenant language to believers who are now God's people, those who were once not a people but have now received mercy.
In the final consummation, the covenant formula is fully fulfilled: God will dwell with humanity, they shall be His people, and He will be their God.
Identical theological characteristic (God's self-revelation) linked to the exodus from Egypt and God's presence.
A direct theological parallel that defines the covenant: The exodus from Egypt is the means of becoming God's people.
Uses the same theological foundation (the exodus from Egypt) as the basis for God's demands on the people.
Expands the theme from historical deliverance to God's eternal faithfulness toward the covenant with the fathers.
Links God's identity as Savior directly to the call to holiness for the people.
Concretizes the concept of 'burdens' from the source verse into liberation from slavery and the yoke.
Clarifies the term 'my people' as a status of servants owned by the Lord.
Completes the promise of the exodus from Egypt with the promise of land inheritance.
Prophetic fulfillment: God's desire that the people should 'know' Him is fulfilled in the heart.
